tweets.text:
Ahead of PCE next week, a reminder to keep an eye on the breadth of price increases.

At Jackson Hole in August, Chair Kevin Warsh said that “over the past 12 months, 54% of goods and services in the PCE basket showed price increases above 3%. This is well below the post-pandemic highs of about 77%, but it remains well above the level of 32% in the two decades that preceded the pandemic.”

Running the same exercise on the CPI across the roughly 180 item categories the BLS publishes, covering about 98% of the basket, yields mixed results.

While 47.2% of categories rose more than 3% from a year earlier in September, the lowest since December and down from 50.6% in August, that compares with an average of 31.7% from 2000 to 2019 although well off the peak of 80.4% in March 2022.

And weighted by share of spending, 62.2% of the basket is rising faster than 3%, the most since September 2025, up from 60.0% in August, as the categories that crossed above 3% included larger ones such as college tuition (+4.00%), hotels (+4.27%), cable, satellite and streaming TV (+3.33%) and motor vehicle repair (+3.55%), while eight of the 17 that fell back below 3% were grocery items.

The share above 5% rose to 23.0% of categories (13.1% of the basket) from 21.0% (11.6%), led by gasoline (+34.17%), hospital services (+5.63%), dental services (+6.02%) and airline fares (+22.45%), while 27.5% of categories are now falling from a year earlier, up from 21.0%.

With the action this week, which Nomura's McElligott said resulted in a "traumatic risk-management unwind" that saw 124 pair trades stop out on the firm's Long/Short monitor including 47 greater than three standard deviations, 26 greater than four and 6 greater than five.  

As ZH notes "a 5-sigma move is supposed to happen roughly once every few thousand years in a normal distribution."

McElligott: To me, a lot of this "Stop-Out / Capitulation" is about Crowding in what had been an unusual year of widespread "High Sharpe Winners" as the "Gifts That Kept Giving" in both -Carry and -Trend....but now, particularly with the abject "Performance Pain" now occuring late in the year during Q4... Traders are now simply forced or incentivized to "Survive Drawdowns" and avoid having their Capital culled ahead of the new year PNL turn...so it's "De-risking and Shut-It-Down" -mode even if some juicy looking trades are there.

ZH: as McElligott shows, the "Reversing" flag is now lit up across nearly every asset class on Nomura's trend monitor: Treasuries across the curve, EUR rates, JGBs, SOFR futures, the S&P, the Nasdaq 100, copper, cocoa, sugar and half the G10 FX board.

Ed Yardeni sees AI investment continuing but tempered by market concerns which has seen the Mag-7 underperform the "other 493" by almost four percent through Thursday's close:

We view market-driven tightening access to capital as healthy for the AI boom, resulting in more efficient capital allocation and reducing over-investment risks. Importantly, we expect the key players to retain financing access. The five major hyperscalers (Amazon, Alphabet, Meta, Microsoft, and Oracle) alone are projected to spend almost $780 billion in 2026. Over each of the following four years, from 2027 through 2030, that figure is expected to exceed $1 trillion annually. Their strong cash flows, balance sheets, and market access should allow them to continue investing in AI.

tweets.text:
As noted in the article from @C_Barraud, investors were bracing for Moody's ratings review on French debt, but the country got some relief after a brutal week which saw the 10-year yield hitting 5% for the first time since 2002, and widening the most against German yields in records dating to 1990.

Heading into Friday most economists expected Moody's to cut France one notch, from Aa3 to A1.  

But it didn't. Instead, Moody's took no rating action, leaving France at Aa3 with a negative outlook. It said this wasn't a credit action and seems to be waiting for more clarity on the budget. It also said higher borrowing costs would need to persist for an extended period to seriously hurt debt sustainability.

The longer view though is sobering. France held AAA ratings from all three major agencies until 2012. Since then it has received 11 downgrades: four from S&P, four from Fitch and three from Moody's. S&P and Fitch now rate France A+, which leaves Moody's as the last of the big three still rating France in the AA tier. 

The negative outlook keeps a downgrade on the table, and S&P reviews France again on Nov 27.

If you're searching for an explanation on why Tech, particularly semiconductors, have been so volatile, you can in part blame the overall negative gamma regime in the market as Tier1Alpha indicated earlier this week.

But semis have an added pseudo-negative-gamma source in the huge amount of assets in leveraged ETFs tied to the space, which must rebalance near the close by buying or selling in the direction of each day’s move.

As Tier1Alpha notes: "we suspect these funds were the largest non-discretionary agents in the market yesterday, especially tied to $SOXL and $TQQQ, which hold a combined $60B in AUM."

They estimate SOXL’s 20% decline forced a $9.5 billion market-on-close (MOC) sell imbalance, while TQQQ “contributed another $6.5 billion in MOC selling.”
